The honest answer to “which AI platform should I choose” is that there is no single winner. Amazon Bedrock dominates on model variety and custom model workflows. Azure AI Foundry wins on compliance breadth and OpenAI exclusivity. Google Vertex AI leads on cost optimization and fine-tuning depth.

claims.normalized_text: Enterprises deploying generative AI across multiple clouds need a governance strategy that unifies security, legal, and operations, according to a March 9, 2026 multi-cloud compliance guide.
CIOs are described as making management of enterprise AI risk across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud a top priority as of early 2026.
US regulators including the SEC and FTC are focusing on regulatory compliance for generative AI, particularly algorithmic bias and financial data transparency.
Cloud governance frameworks described for 2026 rest on automated policy enforcement, continuous visibility, AI and metadata integration, and unified security, cost, and compliance.
AWS Control Tower is described as a native AWS service for governing secure multi-account environments with automated account provisioning, policy enforcement, and compliance management.

Governance tools are described as offering integrated data governance, AI-powered automation, metadata and catalog management, hybrid cloud compatibility, and built-in compliance templates for frameworks such as GDPR and HIPAA.
AI services including Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, and Google Vertex AI are said to accelerate AI usage while also increasing the risk of regulated data leakage into models.
Data residency and sovereignty rules, including GDPR, India DPDP, and emerging sovereignty rules, are described as requiring regional control across hyperscaler regions and availability zones.

Governance tools can govern Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, and Vertex AI usage, redact regulated fields before they reach a foundation model, and provide per-prompt audit logs for EU AI Act and internal review.
Clarip states that it natively supports AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, with region-aware residency enforcement across global cloud regions and end-to-end AI platform governance.

AWS Prescriptive Guidance recommends a governance framework including compliance monitoring, standardized regulatory documentation, metadata tagging for training data, controls for cross-border data and service utilization, and regular third-party audits.

The EU AI Act's August 2026 enforcement deadline is described as approaching, and many enterprises deploying AI in Europe have a data residency strategy while fewer have a genuine data sovereignty strategy.
AI data residency compliance means LLM inference runs in a specified location such as Frankfurt, while data sovereignty means data in that location stays outside the reach of US law enforcement.
For enterprises using US-headquartered cloud providers, data residency compliance and data sovereignty can be in direct legal conflict.

Hyperscale operators led by AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, and Alibaba Cloud represented 64% of the AI data centre market in 2024, according to a December 22, 2025 article citing Precedence Research.

The global data center industry is evolving into a regionally fragmented landscape shaped by AI demand, regulatory pressures, and infrastructure maturity, with more than 2,600 data centers worldwide concentrated unevenly.
In 2025, Europe led with 3,240 data centers, followed by North America with 2,632 and Asia-Pacific with 1,728, while Latin America had 493 and Middle East and Africa had 396.
North America is described as the most advanced data center market, driven by hyperscale leaders such as AWS, Equinix, and Digital Realty.
AWS operates 110 data center locations, Equinix 109, and Digital Realty 86.
In Europe, the data center market is led by Microsoft Azure with 52 locations, AWS with 48, and Google Cloud with 45.
Stricter energy regulations and grid constraints in Europe are described as pushing hyperscalers toward consolidation and high-efficiency deployments.

Asia-Pacific is seeing rapid data center expansion fueled by digitalization in India, ASEAN, Japan, and South Korea, with leading operators including Equinix at 65 locations, Microsoft Azure at 60, AWS at 42, and Zenlayer.
Asia-Pacific is also seeing strong growth in sovereign cloud initiatives driven by data residency and cybersecurity requirements.
Latin America's data center ecosystem is led by Digital Realty, Equinix, AWS, and Oracle, with Digital Realty operating 24 locations, Equinix 9, and AWS and Oracle 7 each.

Middle East and Africa is described as an emerging strategic growth frontier led by Microsoft Azure with 29 locations, Google Cloud with 27, and Cloudflare with 16, benefiting from government-backed digital programs, sovereign cloud policies, and abundant energy.
North America is described as dominating AI-driven hyperscale deployments.
Europe is described as focusing on efficiency under regulatory constraints.
Asia-Pacific is described as balancing hyperscale and sovereign infrastructure.
Latin America is described as relying heavily on colocation.
Middle East and Africa is described as showing the highest reliance on Tier One hyperscalers globally.

The global cloud infrastructure services market exceeded $100 billion in 2022, growing 29.7% to $120.3 billion, with AWS holding 40% share and over $48 billion in revenue and Azure holding 21.5% and nearly $26 billion.
Alibaba Cloud was described as ranking third with $9.28 billion in revenue and limited growth outside China, leading to a decision to spin it off into a separate entity.
Google Cloud was described as ranking fourth with over $9 billion in revenue and 41% growth in 2022, aided by sovereign cloud investments and expanded partner programs.
Huawei was described as reaching the top five global IaaS providers with 4.4% market share and $5.25 billion in revenue.
Gartner's Sid Nag emphasized that generative AI is pivotal in driving cloud market expansion, with new opportunities related to sovereignty, ethics, privacy, and sustainability.
Hyperscalers held 37% of worldwide data center capacity, non-hyperscale colocation 23%, and on-premise data centers 40%, with hyperscale capacity projected to nearly double over the next five years.

Amazon Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry, and Google Vertex AI have matured from model hosting services into full-stack AI development platforms with agent orchestration, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, fine-tuning workflows, and enterprise compliance controls.

A comparison concludes there is no single winner among Amazon Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry, and Google Vertex AI; Amazon Bedrock dominates on model variety and custom model workflows, Azure AI Foundry wins on compliance breadth and OpenAI exclusivity, and Google Vertex AI leads on cost optimization and fine-tuning depth.

The most common pairing is described as Azure AI Foundry for GPT models and Microsoft ecosystem integration plus Amazon Bedrock for Claude and a broader model catalog, while Google Vertex AI tends to be either the primary platform or not used at all.

Amazon Bedrock launched in April 2023 as a model marketplace, giving AWS customers API access to foundation models from Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, Cohere, and Amazon's Nova family without managing infrastructure; by 2026 it had added AgentCore, Guardrails, Knowledge Bases, and provisioned throughput.
Amazon Bedrock is described as allowing Claude, Llama, Mistral, and Nova to be run behind a single API endpoint.
Region availability is listed as 17 regions on six continents for Amazon Bedrock, 14 regions for Azure AI Foundry, and 22 regions for Google Vertex AI.

FedRAMP authorization is listed as yes for Amazon Bedrock in East and West, Azure AI Foundry in Azure Government, and Google Vertex AI in GovCloud; HIPAA BAA, SOC 2 Type II, and ISO 27001 are listed as yes for all three.
Primary differentiators are listed as model marketplace breadth for Amazon Bedrock, OpenAI exclusivity for Azure AI Foundry, and a Gemini plus TPU vertical stack for Google Vertex AI.
Xenoss states that AWS offers unmatched model diversity and enterprise compliance, while Azure delivers deep productivity and governance integration.

CloudOptimo describes Amazon Bedrock as simplifying access to top models with flexibility and scalability, Azure OpenAI as prioritizing enterprise AI delivery with strong model access and ecosystem ties, and Google Vertex AI as empowering technical teams to go deep into AI customization and experimentation.

CloudOptimo says Google Vertex AI provides direct access to Gemini and PaLM, native multimodal capabilities, and end-to-end MLOps tools, but has less variety in foundation models compared to Amazon Bedrock and pricing that can be complex and harder to predict at scale.

Executives are increasingly driving AI initiatives, with 81% leading adoption compared to 53% last year, while 44% of companies identify infrastructure limitations as their primary obstacle and nearly 74% of organizations opt for managed cloud services.

Google Vertex AI is described as suitable for data-intensive, analytics-driven enterprises because native integrations into BigQuery, Dataflow, and Looker allow AI training, deployment, and querying without transferring data across systems.
Model Garden provides access to third-party models including Anthropic's Claude via a partnership, and Google's Agent Builder powered by the Vertex AI Agent Development Kit handles agentic workflows.
